passage:
Madhuri, I owe you an apology for yesterday, and an explanation. I've been sleeping maybe five hours a night for two weeks. Chemistry till midnight, then I scroll till one-thirty because it's the only time that feels like mine. Then the alarm at six-thirty.
And I've turned into someone I don't like. I snapped at Mummy about the tiffin. I cried in the bathroom because I got a seven instead of a nine on a quiz, which is ridiculous. And yesterday, when you joked about my hair, I basically bit your head off.
I thought I was just becoming a horrible person. Then on Saturday I slept till ten by accident, and the whole day I was fine. Normal. Nice, even.
So it's not me. Well, it's me, but it's me on no sleep. I'm Darshan, and I'm trying a phone-in-the-kitchen rule at eleven.

qa.q: What score did Darshan get on the quiz?
qa.a: A seven instead of a nine.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel about the snapping and crying before Saturday?
qa.a: Darshan felt ashamed and confused, believing the cause was becoming a horrible person.

qa.q: Why is the phone-in-the-kitchen rule a good step?
qa.a: It cuts the late scrolling so Darshan sleeps more, and Saturday showed that rest makes the whole day fine.

qa.q: How might Madhuri have felt when Darshan snapped over the hair joke?
qa.a: Madhuri was probably hurt and surprised, having only been joking.

grounding: Shows a teenager staying up late becoming irritable and teary, and mistaking lost sleep for a personality flaw.

Monday. Jatin had gone to bed at 2 am after gaming, and at school he stared at the whiteboard as if it were in another language. When Lalremsiami Ma'am asked him to read aloud, he slammed the book and said, "Why always me?"
Wednesday. After class Ma'am kept him back. "You're not usually like this. How are you sleeping?" Jatin shrugged, then admitted it: two, sometimes three. She didn't lecture. "Try one week of midnight. Then tell me how Monday feels."
The next Monday. Jatin had been in bed by twelve all week. He read his paragraph aloud, stumbled on one word, laughed at himself and kept going.

qa.a: At 2 am, after gaming.

qa.q: Why did Jatin slam the book and snap at Ma'am?
qa.a: He was exhausted and irritable from going to bed at 2 am, so a small request felt like too much.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She asked about sleep instead of scolding, and suggested one week of midnight bedtimes as a test.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami Ma'am read the slammed book?
qa.a: Ma'am saw it as unusual for Jatin and wondered about tiredness rather than simple rudeness.

grounding: Shows a teenager's late nights making him foggy and reactive, and more sleep bringing back his steadier self.

Akash, you think you invented staying up late? At fifteen I read novels under the quilt with a torch till two, every night of the monsoon. By August I was a monster. I shouted at my little brother for touching my pencil box. I cried in class because the teacher called my handwriting untidy. My mother thought I had become proud and rude, and I believed her. I thought it was simply who I was.
Then I got the flu and slept for three days straight. When I got up, everything was lighter. My brother, the pencil box, the teacher: none of it seemed worth a tear.
That was when I understood it was not my character. It was the torch. Your Swati Nani put the torch away at ten after that, mostly.

qa.a: Novels.

qa.q: What did young Swati believe about her own moods?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, believing her mother that she had become proud and rude, as if it were her character.

qa.q: Which moment in the story changed Swati's understanding?
qa.a: Sleeping for three days with the flu made everything feel lighter, showing the moods came from the torch-lit nights, not her character.

qa.q: How did Swati's mother see the change in her?
qa.a: Her mother thought Swati had become proud and rude, without seeing the lost sleep behind it.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose late nights made her irritable and tearful, mistaken for a flaw in her character.

Raghav had a different schedule taped to his cupboard: study blocks till nine, dinner with the family, a twenty-minute walk round the colony, lights off by eleven. His mother had grumbled at first. "Only till nine? Pradeep studies all night!"
On the morning of the maths paper, Raghav walked to the bus stop feeling slow but clear. Pradeep was there already, eyes red. "I did the whole of integration last night," he said. "Now I can't remember the first formula."
Raghav handed him a biscuit. In the exam hall the formulas came back to Raghav one by one, like people walking into a room.

qa.a: Raghav felt slow but calm and clear-headed after keeping the schedule all week.

qa.q: Which parts of Raghav's routine protected his recall?
qa.a: Sleep by eleven, dinner with the family and a twenty-minute walk kept him rested, so the formulas came back in the hall.

At the team huddle in the customer-support office, the manager asked who could cover the Sunday shift. Deepika looked at Sarika. Sarika always said yes.
"Not this Sunday," Sarika said. "Or any Sunday this month. I've made Sundays my day off, a real one. Phone on silent, lunch with my grandmother, no work messages."
There was a small silence. Deepika raised her eyebrows. "Since when?"

qa.a: Sarika got so tired she cried at a customer's thank-you message.

qa.q: What does Deepika's quiet question over tea suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Deepika admired Sarika's clear boundary and wished she could protect her own rest, perhaps feeling a little envious.

qa.q: What made Sarika's refusal work?
qa.a: Sarika stated the rest day plainly, gave a reason, and offered Saturday evening instead.

qa.q: How might the manager see Sarika's new rule?
qa.a: The manager seems to accept it easily, nodding and moving on, perhaps because Sarika offered another shift.

grounding: Shows a young worker protecting a real weekly day off as prevention rather than waiting to collapse.

Dear Gargi,
You asked what changed. It's boring, honestly. I built rest into the week before I needed it.
Wednesday evenings: no laptop after seven. I cook something slow, usually rajma, and eat at the table, not at my desk.
Saturday mornings: the long walk to the flower market, phone left at home. I used to think I'd miss something important. I never have.

Come walk with me on Saturday? Flowers, chai, no phones.

qa.a: Chinmay feels calmer and more content, finishing books again instead of resting only when sick.

Yamini, people at the depot laugh that I, Chetan, am the only engineer who leaves at six. Here's why. In my first year at the metro depot I worked every weekend. I thought rest was something you earned after the big project. The project ended, and I spent my first free week in bed with a fever, too tired to enjoy a thing.

Dear Nikita,
You asked how I made the job decision so calmly. I didn't, at first. For two weeks my head was all noise: my parents' opinions, my manager's offer, forty tabs of salary comparisons.
Then I started walking to the lake at six every morning, without my phone. Forty minutes. The first few days my hand kept reaching for my pocket. By the fourth morning my thoughts started lining up, one after another, instead of shouting at once.
On the seventh walk I realised I didn't want the promotion if it meant moving away from Amma. That was it. Clear.
I still walk every morning. It's the only time nobody is asking me anything. Try it before your own big decision?
Amandeep

qa.q: How long is Amandeep's morning walk?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel during the first two weeks?
qa.a: Amandeep felt overwhelmed, with a head full of noise from opinions, offers and tabs.

qa.q: Why did the phone-free walks help Amandeep decide?
qa.a: Without messages, thoughts lined up one at a time until it was clear the promotion wasn't worth moving away from Amma.

qa.q: How might Nikita take the suggestion to try it?
qa.a: Nikita might find it reassuring and practical, coming from someone who was just as overwhelmed.

grounding: Shows a young professional using a device-free morning walk to sort thoughts and reach a clear decision.

passage:
Alka, you asked on the show how I handle the chaos of running a school canteen at twenty-four. Honestly? On Tuesdays and Fridays, before the gate opens, I sit alone on the back steps for fifteen minutes with a cup of tea and no phone. The cooks know not to call me.
It started last year when I was drowning: suppliers ringing, parents complaining, a cook quitting. I kept making decisions in the middle of the noise, and half of them were wrong. One morning I just sat on the steps and let everything come in order. Within ten minutes I knew: drop the late supplier, hire the cook's cousin, move the menu board.
Now those fifteen minutes are where I make every big call. I'm Mridul, and the steps are my office.

qa.q: When does Mridul sit on the back steps?
qa.a: On Tuesdays and Fridays, before the gate opens.

qa.q: How was Mridul feeling last year before starting the practice?
qa.a: Mridul felt overwhelmed, drowning in calls and complaints and making decisions in the noise, half of them wrong.

qa.q: What makes Mridul's fifteen minutes effective?
qa.a: They're scheduled, device-free and protected, since the cooks know not to call, which gives thoughts time to settle into order.

qa.q: What might the cooks think about the fifteen minutes?
qa.a: The cooks probably respect it, knowing that's when Mridul sorts things out and that decisions come clearer afterwards.

grounding: Shows a young professional deliberately taking quiet, device-free time that sorts thoughts and sharpens decisions.

passage:
June. Gargi noticed Keerthana skip the Friday dinner again, with a thumbs-up and "next time!" It was the third "next time" in a row.
August. Keerthana's replies had shrunk to single words. When Gargi called, it rang out. Her photos had stopped. Gargi almost let it go; everyone was busy. Instead she sent a message: "No need to reply. Just thinking of you. Chai on Sunday if you feel like it, my place, no plans."
September. On Sunday Keerthana turned up, hair uncombed, and sat on Gargi's floor for two hours. At first she said little. Then: "I've been in a bad patch since the job ended. I didn't want to be a downer." Gargi made more chai. Before Keerthana left, they set another Sunday, and Keerthana said she'd look for a counsellor.

qa.q: What did Gargi offer in the August message?
qa.a: Chai on Sunday at Gargi's place, with no plans and no need to reply.

qa.q: What made Gargi decide not to let it go in August?
qa.a: Gargi felt worried, noticing single-word replies, unanswered calls and stopped photos after three "next time"s.

qa.q: Why did Gargi's message work?
qa.a: It was gentle and low-pressure, asking for nothing and offering an easy, open invitation.

qa.q: Why had Keerthana been pulling away?
qa.a: Keerthana was in a bad patch since the job ended and didn't want to be a downer.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone slowly declining invitations and replying less, and reaching out gently.

passage:
Saurabh, sit. You say your friend Kunal has stopped answering? Let me tell you about Leela. When I was twenty-four, teaching in Pune, Leela and I shared everything. Then her father died, and slowly she stopped coming to the Sunday market with us. First she said she was tired. Then she said nothing.
I told myself she wanted space. For two months I waited. That was my mistake.
One evening I just went to her door with a packet of her favourite jalebis. I didn't ask questions. I said, "I'm here for an hour, if you want company." She opened the door. We sat and ate and hardly talked. I went back every Thursday. Months later she told me those Thursdays were the only thing she looked forward to.
So, Saurabh, don't wait two months like your Irawati Aaji did.

qa.q: What did Irawati bring to Leela's door?
qa.a: A packet of Leela's favourite jalebis.

qa.q: How does Irawati now feel about those two months of waiting?
qa.a: Irawati feels regretful, calling the two months of waiting a mistake.

qa.q: Which choice in the story made the difference for Leela?
qa.a: Going to Leela's door with jalebis and a no-questions offer of company, then returning every Thursday.

qa.q: What did the Thursday visits mean to Leela?
qa.a: They were the only thing Leela looked forward to during that time.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone slowly withdrawing after a loss, and gentle, low-pressure visits making a difference.

passage:
Urmila was working night shifts at the hospital in Nagpur, and her friend Sahil lived four hundred kilometres away in Indore. Their weekly calls had slipped to monthly, then to nothing. Lately his replies in the group chat were just a heart, if anything. He had skipped the online quiz night three times.
Urmila had no time to visit, and she was usually asleep when others were awake. But on a slow night at 4 am she recorded a short voice note: "No need to reply. I miss your terrible jokes. I'll send you one voice note every Sunday, even if you don't answer."
She kept it up for five Sundays. On the sixth, a reply came: "Sorry I went quiet. Things have been heavy. Can we talk on your day off?" Urmila set an alarm for the afternoon so she wouldn't sleep through it.

qa.q: How many Sundays did Urmila send voice notes before Sahil replied?
qa.a: Five Sundays; the reply came on the sixth.

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling when she recorded the first voice note?
qa.a: Urmila was probably worried about Sahil and missed him, noticing the single hearts, the skipped quiz nights and the silence.

qa.q: Why did voice notes suit this situation?
qa.a: They were low-pressure and fit Urmila's night shifts and the distance, asking for no reply while showing steady care.

qa.q: What was it like for Sahil to receive them?
qa.a: Sahil was going through a heavy time, and the steady notes seem to have made it easier to reach back and ask to talk.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone replying less and skipping plans, and reaching out in a gentle, low-pressure way.

passage:
During garden time at the kindergarten, Manjula crouched by the neem tree and stopped moving. A line of ants was carrying tiny white crumbs into a crack in the ground.
"Sudha Ma'am! Look! Where are they going? Do they have a house? Is there a mummy ant?"
Sudha knelt down beside her in the dust. "Let's watch and see."
They watched together. An ant dropped its crumb, and another picked it up. Manjula gasped. "They're helping!" Two more children came to look, then three.
Soon half the class was lying on their tummies in a row, whispering, and Sudha was whispering too.

qa.q: What were the ants carrying?
qa.a: Tiny white crumbs.

qa.q: What does Manjula's gasp suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was amazed and delighted to see one ant help another.

qa.q: How did Sudha deepen Manjula's wonder?
qa.a: She knelt in the dust and watched with her, saying "Let's watch and see" instead of answering everything.

qa.q: Why might the other children have come over?
qa.a: They were probably curious, drawn by Manjula's excitement and the teacher kneeling in the dust.

grounding: Shows a child's wide-eyed wonder at an ant line spreading to others when an adult shares the gaze.

passage:
Monday. Thunder cracked over the building, and Sonali ran to the window instead of hiding. "Mumma, where does the noise come from?" Himani came and stood beside her. They watched the sky flash.
Wednesday. Sonali asked a hundred questions at breakfast. Why is lightning first? Why is thunder slow? Himani said, "Let's count between them next time."
Friday. Another storm. Sonali and Himani sat by the window, counting. "One, two, three, BOOM!" Sonali shrieked with joy, then whispered, "It's big, Mumma. The sky is so big."

qa.q: What did Sonali and Himani do during Friday's storm?
qa.a: They sat by the window counting between the flash and the thunder.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel as she whispered "The sky is so big"?
qa.a: Sonali felt awe, thrilled and amazed at how big the sky is.

qa.q: What did Himani do that fed Sonali's wonder?
qa.a: Himani stood beside her at the window and suggested counting, sharing the gaze instead of shooing her away.

qa.q: What might the storms have been like for Himani?
qa.a: For Himani they became a shared, joyful time with her daughter instead of something to hide from.

grounding: Shows a child's awe at thunder, with endless questions, deepened by a parent who watches alongside.

passage:
The bus to Nani's village broke down on the highway after dark, and everyone had to get off and wait beside the fields. Dhruv, five, was tired and cross. Then his cousin Hrithik pointed up.
There were more stars than Dhruv had ever seen. In the city there were five, maybe six. Here the sky was full, as if someone had spilled sugar.
"Whoa," Dhruv breathed. "Are they all real? Who made them? Can we go there?"
Hrithik lay back on the grass next to him. "I don't know everything. Let's just look."
Dhruv lay still for a long time. When the new bus came, he didn't want to get on.

qa.q: How many stars could Dhruv usually see in the city?
qa.a: Five, maybe six.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he breathed "Whoa"?
qa.a: Dhruv felt awe and wonder, amazed at a sky full of stars.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do that helped Dhruv's wonder grow?
qa.a: He pointed up, lay on the grass beside him and said "Let's just look" instead of explaining everything.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel seeing Dhruv not want to get on the bus?
qa.a: Hrithik probably felt amused and happy that a breakdown had turned into something magical for his cousin.

grounding: Shows a child's simple, bodily awe at a starry sky, deepened by an older cousin who shares the gaze.
